title: small-batch-latency-cost-scenarios-draft
summary: Scenario-driven recommendations for small-batch workloads: proposed default configs, cost/latency estimates, rollout plan, and spreadsheet pointers to run cost sensitivity sweeps.
body:
Purpose
This is a working recommendation memo for how we should set defaults and guardrails for low-latency, low-throughput (small-batch) inference workloads in Redwood Optimize. The goal: reduce per-token $ cost while keeping p95 latency within customer SLOs for interactive flows. This draft is intentionally scenario-focused so product and runtime teams can test tradeoffs in the attached cost-model spreadsheet.

Background and motivation
- Many customer workloads are small-batch by design: chat UX, single-turn generation, short embeddings calls, or webhooks that prefer low tail latency over absolute throughput.
- Prior art in product/optimize focused on batching heuristics and broad quantization guidance. This memo complements that with a small-batch-first policy, concrete numeric defaults, and an experiment plan to measure quality regressions across quant levels.

Key constraints and assumptions (for the scenarios below)
- Typical request sequence lengths: 16–256 tokens for chat/generation; 8–128 for embeddings/reranking.
- Target latency SLOs: p50 < 40ms, p95 < 250ms for interactive customers (latency tiers configurable).
- Hardware profile: A100/A10x or equivalent on Dedicated; smaller GPUs for Private (e.g., T4, H100 for heavy models).
- Model families: opt-family and llama-derivatives (7B, 13B, 70B). We provide examples across size bands.

Scenario matrix and recommended defaults (small-batch-focused)
Format: scenario name — workload pattern — recommended batching policy — caching — quantization — expected cost delta (vs baseline fp16) — rationale
1) micro-interactive (chat widgets) — arrival: 1–10 rps, median seq 64 tokens — batching: continuous small-batches with max_batch_size 8, max_wait_ms 6, prefer latency-first scheduling — caching: prefix/KV caching enabled for repeated prompts, short TTLs (60s) for session reuse, client-side conversation pinning recommended — quantization: nf4/4-bit for 7B/13B when quality tests pass; 8-bit for 70B as default — expected cost delta: -25% (7B nf4), -15% (13B nf4), -12% (70B int8) — rationale: small batch sizes keep latency low while quantization yields unit-cost savings. Short TTLs capture immediate session reuse without stale cache inflation.

2) heartbeat-embeddings (periodic single doc embedding) — arrival: bursty single calls, median seq 64 tokens — batching: prefer immediate processing (max_wait_ms 2) and opportunistic background coalescing for <50ms — caching: embedding cache for exact text hashes with long TTL (7d) and dedupe layer — quantization: use 8-bit or fp16 for embeddings kernels (avoid 4-bit unless validated) — expected cost delta: -10 to -30% depending on cache hit rate — rationale: embeddings are high-benefit for caching; quantization affects vector fidelity so prefer conservative defaults.

3) low-volume reranking API — arrival: 0.5–5 rps, multi-candidate scoring, median seq 32 tokens — batching: group candidates per request (intra-request batching) and allow small inter-request coalescing up to max_batch_size 16 with max_wait_ms 8 — caching: short-lived per-query cache (30s) for repeated queries; cache keys include candidate set fingerprint — quantization: 8-bit for 13B, test nf4 on 7B — expected cost delta: -18% typical — rationale: intra-request batching is more efficient and avoids cross-tenant noise; quantization here is lower risk because scoring is tolerant.

4) fallback cascade mode (reliability-first) — arrival: variable spikes — batching: latency-first at edge; route to larger-batch scaled pool only when the model pool indicates throughput headroom — caching: aggressive prefix caching on primary route; fallback uses non-cached but lower-cost variant — quantization: prefer dynamic selection: fp16 for primary, int8 for fallback — expected cost delta: depends on fallback ratio; aim to keep cost < +5% vs baseline while improving availability — rationale: protect p95 latency while reducing cost by steering non-critical requests to quantized fallbacks.

Numeric default table (quick reference)
- max_batch_size: 8 (interactive), 16 (rerank with candidates), 32 (background batch jobs)
- max_wait_ms: 6 (interactive), 8–12 (rerank), 30–100 (background)
- batching_strategy: latency_first for interactive, throughput_first for background
- prefix_cache_ttl: 60s (session reuse), 30s (rerank), 7d (embeddings exact match)
- kv_cache_enabled: true for decoder-greedy and chat; false for short-lived stateless transforms unless safe
- quant_default_7B: nf4 if eval pass, else int8
- quant_default_13B: nf4 recommended with regression monitoring, else int8
- quant_default_70B: int8 by default; 4-bit only behind gated experiments
- quant_quality_gate: A/B test with ROUGE/LLM-eval and human-in-the-loop checks; rollout only if automated eval delta < 0.8% and human baseline OK

Quality and monitoring plan
- Define a small standard prompt set (~200 prompts) covering: factual QA, instruction following, code completion, and toxic content regression checks. Store in the linked spreadsheet under tab: "small-batch-eval-suite".
- Automated regressions: trigger alerts when model output similarity (embedding distance) deviates > 0.12 on average and content metrics drop more than 1%.
- Production canary: 5% traffic to quantized variant for 48–72 hours with manual review checkpoints.
- Metrics to track: p50/p95 latency, token throughput, per-token cost, inference error rate (timeouts, decode failures), human quality score sampling.

Cost-model spreadsheet guidance
- The attached spreadsheet (linked_artifacts) contains multiple sheets: baseline of fp16 throughput/cost, quantized kernel performance, cache hit simulation, and sensitivity sweeps for batch size vs latency. Run sweeps with the customer's sequence-length distribution where possible.
- Quick heuristics from the spreadsheet: small sequence lengths favor smaller max_wait_ms; a 20% cache hit rate on embeddings can reduce effective embedding spend by >50% depending on card packing.

Operational guardrails and rollout checklist
- Start with conservative defaults: int8 for 13B/70B; nf4 for 7B only after eval pass.
- Canary and monitor both quality and latency. If p95 increases >10% or quality delta >1.0% revert automatically to prior model config.
- Provide a per-customer toggle labeled "Aggressive Cost Savings" that applies a recommended bundle: lower max_wait_ms, aggressive quantization, and extended cache TTLs. Require explicit customer opt-in and signoff for any quantization below 8-bit.

Developer/Runtime integration notes
- Expose two high-level policy presets in the Console and API: small-batch-interactive (defaults above) and small-batch-background (favor batching). Keep these editable per-route.
- Runtime needs a lightweight admission controller for: (a) sequence-length histogram sampling, (b) tracking per-route cache hit/miss rates, (c) auto-throttling when p95 exceeds threshold.

Open questions and experiments to run
- How does nf4 on 13B perform on instruction-following relative to int8? (Experimental — assign to Applied ML sprint 10).
- Is there measurable client-side batching gain if SDKs provide a soft coalescing hint? Prototype in dev sandbox.
- Best TTL defaults for multi-tenant prefix caching without creating cache thrash across high-cardinality prompts? Run a 2-week simulation with synthetic traffic.

Action items and owners
- Add the small-batch eval suite to the central spreadsheet and populate with ~200 prompts (owner: Marta Ruiz, due 2025-03-05).
- Run an nf4 vs int8 AB test on 7B and 13B across the eval suite (owner: Samir Gupta, due 2025-03-12).
- Implement the two policy presets in Console (owner: Ethan Park, due 2025-03-19).
- Wire cost-model sensitivity sweeps into the Optimize product page so customers can preview tradeoffs (owner: Priya Natarajan, PM, due 2025-03-26).

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally prescriptive; please comment if a default appears too aggressive for Private deployments or for customers with strict quality needs.
- If you have benchmark artifacts (kernel perf numbers) not captured in the linked spreadsheet, paste links in the Google Sheet in the "kernel-benchmarks" tab.

Appendix: Example expected impact numbers (rough, from internal microbenchmarks)
- 7B nf4: ~2.5x token/sec vs fp16 on small batches, cost -30%–40% depending on packing.
- 13B nf4: ~1.6x token/sec vs fp16 on small batches, cost -15%–25%.
- 70B int8: ~1.2x token/sec vs fp16, smaller quality delta than 4-bit on long-form completions.

Unresolveds
- Precise thresholds for automated rollback. Propose: p95 latency increase >10% OR sampled human-error-rate >1.0% triggers rollback. Feedback?

End of draft
notes: This is a working Drive doc; use the linked spreadsheet for numbers. Keep discussion in the Optimize channel and reference this file when creating PRs to runtime or console repos.
